intro: Ngāhinapōuri is a farming village in the Waikato, south-west of Hamilton, with its hall, its school and a memorial park side by side on Kakaramea Road. The park was given to the district in 1946 in memory of a young pilot, and thirty-four trees were planted in it for the local men who served in the Second World War. A reader sent us a plane from it.

trees.story:
In 1946 Neil and Gracie Reid gave five and a quarter acres of land at Ngāhinapōuri, south-west of Hamilton, to the people of the district in memory of their son Stewart, a pilot officer killed on active service in 1942. The ground became Stewart Reid Memorial Park, and thirty-four trees were planted in it, one for each man from the district who went away to the Second World War. A reader sent us this plane from the park.

It is a London plane, and its trunk is what holds the eye: smooth, swelling at the foot and patched all over in olive, cream and grey where the old bark has flaked away. Above head height it forks into long pale limbs under a broad summer crown of maple-shaped leaves. More trees stand in a line along the edge of the grass, and at the left of the reader's picture is the stepped concrete base the park's flagpole stands on.

Whether this plane is one of the thirty-four memorial trees we do not know, because the record we found does not name their species. If you know, or know whose name it carries, tell us here.

The village war memorial stands in the same park. Walk the line of trees from the flagpole and stop under this one.

question_meta: A London plane in Stewart Reid Memorial Park at Ngāhinapōuri in the Waikato, the park given in 1946 and planted with 34 memorial trees.
question_answer: The Plane of Stewart Reid Memorial Park grows in the memorial park on Kakaramea Road in Ngāhinapōuri, beside the hall and the school. The park is public and free.
question_context: Stewart Reid Memorial Park is the village green of Ngāhinapōuri, a farming district of the Waikato south-west of Hamilton. Neil and Gracie Reid gave the land, five and a quarter acres, to the people of Ngāhinapōuri and Tuhikaramea on 1 March 1946, in memory of their son Stewart, a pilot officer killed on active service in February 1942. Thirty-four trees were planted in the park, one for each man from the district who went away to serve in the Second World War, and a plaque lists the names of the men they honour. The village war memorial stands in the park too, and a flagpole rises from a stepped concrete base. A reader sent us the plane on this page from the park: a London plane with a smooth trunk flaking in patches of olive, cream and grey, at the head of a line of trees along the grass. Whether it is one of the thirty-four we cannot yet say. If you know which trees were planted for which men, tell us.

faq.q: Can I visit The Plane of Stewart Reid Memorial Park?
faq.a: Yes. It stands in a public memorial park on Kakaramea Road in Ngāhinapōuri, free to walk into.

faq.q: Why were trees planted in Stewart Reid Memorial Park?
faq.a: The park was given to the district in 1946 in memory of pilot officer Stewart Reid, and 34 trees were planted in it, one for each local man who served in the Second World War.

faq.q: Is the plane one of the memorial trees?
faq.a: We do not know yet. The record we found does not name the species of the 34 memorial trees; if you know, tell us on the tree's page.
